claims.claim: Hatch cites the Mosaic's first-page narratorial claim that writers of history often seek the dramatic over the truth.
claims.source: Jillian Hatch, 'The Creative Construction of History in Guy Gavriel Kay's The Sarantine Mosaic' (University of Calgary undergraduate paper, 2005)
claims.quote: writers of history often seek the dramatic over the truth

claims.claim: Hatch notes the narrative is focused on both leaders and the 'common' man, unlike traditional history.
claims.source: Jillian Hatch, 'The Creative Construction of History in Guy Gavriel Kay's The Sarantine Mosaic' (University of Calgary undergraduate paper, 2005)
claims.quote: focused on both the affairs of leaders

claims.claim: Cawsey's introduction states Kay includes only supernatural elements the depicted society believed, presented from the inside-out so the setting renders these beliefs as true.
claims.source: Kathy Cawsey, 'Magic and Realism: An Interview with Guy Gavriel Kay', The Dalhousie Review (2021), pp. 307-317

claims.claim: Cawsey reports Kay's Bagehot-derived principle of leaving the workings of magic unexplained, since characters would not analyse their beliefs.
claims.source: Kathy Cawsey, 'Magic and Realism: An Interview with Guy Gavriel Kay', The Dalhousie Review (2021), pp. 307-317
claims.quote: leaves the exact details of the workings of magic unexplained

claims.feature: great events at the personal level
claims.claim: Kay tells Cawsey the death of a far-off emperor means less to a farmer than his hired hand's broken leg, the personal running through his fiction.
claims.source: Kathy Cawsey, 'Magic and Realism: An Interview with Guy Gavriel Kay', The Dalhousie Review (2021), pp. 307-317
claims.quote: The death of the emperor far off means far less

claims.claim: Kay tells Cawsey he has become even more engaged with giving value to lives that go unrecorded, drawing on recent social history.
claims.source: Kathy Cawsey, 'Magic and Realism: An Interview with Guy Gavriel Kay', The Dalhousie Review (2021), pp. 307-317
claims.quote: giving value to lives that often go unrecorded

claims.claim: Kay tells Cawsey he has a drive towards complexity, even celebrating it, against the cultural tendencies of the day.
claims.source: Kathy Cawsey, 'Magic and Realism: An Interview with Guy Gavriel Kay', The Dalhousie Review (2021), pp. 307-317
claims.quote: a drive towards complexity, I think—even towards celebrating it

claims.claim: Kay tells Cawsey the absence of a specific time and place lets readers see a story as not tied to one place, at the cost of readers who want to be educated.
claims.source: Kathy Cawsey, 'Magic and Realism: An Interview with Guy Gavriel Kay', The Dalhousie Review (2021), pp. 307-317
claims.quote: the absence of a specific time and place

claims.claim: Kay lists Frazer, Graves, Campbell, the Mabinogion, Malory and the Poetic Edda as the steeping of the first trilogy.
claims.source: Kathy Cawsey, 'Magic and Realism: An Interview with Guy Gavriel Kay', The Dalhousie Review (2021), pp. 307-317
claims.quote: so much steeped in myth, legend, and folklore

claims.claim: Kay: fantasy detaches the tale from a narrow context and erodes prejudices, so a story cannot be read as only about Spain seven hundred years ago.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Home and Away' (keynote essay; shorter version in The Globe and Mail, fall 1999) — Wayback copy of the Bright Weavings text
claims.quote: detaches the tale from a narrow context

claims.claim: Kay answers Henry James: treating the past as fantasy acknowledges the impossibility of recovering past world-views, a way of being honest about limitations.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Home and Away' (keynote essay; shorter version in The Globe and Mail, fall 1999) — Wayback copy of the Bright Weavings text
claims.quote: a way of being honest about limitations

claims.claim: Kay says inventing a man based on El Cid but clearly not him demonstrates a measure of appropriate distance and declares his guesswork.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Home and Away' (keynote essay; shorter version in The Globe and Mail, fall 1999) — Wayback copy of the Bright Weavings text
claims.quote: demonstrating a measure of appropriate distance

claims.claim: Kay adopts Douglas Barbour's phrase for what fantasy can do.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Home and Away' (keynote essay; shorter version in The Globe and Mail, fall 1999) — Wayback copy of the Bright Weavings text
claims.quote: The kind of escape that brings you home

claims.claim: Kay says for The Last Light of the Sun he tried to shape language and a form of telling using elements from the sagas to show a less urbane world.
claims.source: Teresa Basinski Eckford, 'Parallel Universes: Guy Gavriel Kay reflects on twenty years of alternative history', Historical Novels Review (Nov 2004)
claims.quote: shape language and a form of telling the tale

claims.claim: Kay names Dorothy Dunnett's ability to reveal character within and through action scenes as unmatched and a model.
claims.source: Teresa Basinski Eckford, 'Parallel Universes: Guy Gavriel Kay reflects on twenty years of alternative history', Historical Novels Review (Nov 2004)
claims.quote: reveal and showcase character within and through action scenes
